title: yesmcp: agent-native booking, the human keeps the click
pitch: A real booking service an in-browser agent can use through WebMCP. It checks live availability and prepares a booking. The page then asks the human to press Confirm.
about_excerpt: A real booking service an in-browser agent can use through WebMCP. It checks live availability and prepares a booking. The page then asks the human to press Confirm. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What it is yesmcp ( https://yesmcp.com ) is a live business. It builds companies their own MCP connectors so their customers can book, order and ask directly inside AI chats. Its own site now practices what it sells at a deeper level: the site itself is agent-native through WebMCP. The home page registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Every other page registers four of them: the entrance gate and the demo driver exist only on the home page, and a tool that cannot work on a page is never registered there. get_services : the authored services catalog. The answer carries an explicit degradation flag, so an agent never presents a stub as the catalog. check_availability : genuinely bookable 30-minute windows with slot ids. Every label carries an explicit UTC offset, never a bare wall-clock time. book_consult : prepares a REAL booking, then opens a confirmation card on the page. The request is submitted only after the human clicks Confirm. Decline is a first-class answer returned to the agent, not an error. get_live_status : live proof numbers from the production connector. answer_entrance_check : the site asks arriving visitors one question at the door. This answers it, so an agent can open the page for its human instead of stalling at a dialog it cannot see past. drive_demo (home page only): drives the interactive hero chat demo through the same controls a finger taps, so the visitor can watch the story the agent is telling. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP A services business's page is exactly where "humans and agents together" stops being a slogan. The agent does the tedious part: find the catalog, check the calendar, fill the form. The human does the human part: decide, and press the one button that commits their calendar and their inbox. Before WebMCP an in-browser agent had to guess at our DOM and click blind. One redesign and it breaks. With WebMCP it gets the same honest API our own page uses, and the page stays a normal website for everyone else. No modelContext API means no behavior at all, so all of this is progressive enhancement. How it creates a better user experience The visitor never has to translate between two systems. They say what they want in their own words, the agent turns that into two tool calls, and what comes back on screen is the server's own label for the slot, not the agent's paraphrase of it. The one irreversible step stays with the person: a card rendered by the site itself, with a button the agent cannot press. What people and agents can do together that was hard before A visitor tells their browser agent "find me a slot Thursday afternoon and set up the call". The agent checks real availability, fills the booking, and the visitor confirms with one click on a card the site rendered. The confirmation email and the owner's notification run the same production path every other door uses. The agent can also show things, not only tell them. drive_demo replays the landing's scripted chat story (browse, pick a time, booked, reschedule) in front of the visitor, driven through the same controls a finger would tap. It is labelled as a scripted demo, and the real tools sit right beside it. This is not a prototype It is a running production service. Bookings are atomic: the confirmation email is sent inside the transaction, so if the send fails the slot is released. A booking nobody was told about is not a booking. There is rate limiting, an origin allow-list on the browser endpoints, a public status endpoint reporting since 2026-08-21, and a test suite that runs green on every change. The public counter deliberately excludes bookings made from test domains, so the number it reports can only ever mean real customers. The demo booking recorded for this submission does not inflate it. The same capability already runs as a remote MCP server at https://mcp.yesmcp.com/mcp , which works today from Claude and ChatGPT. WebMCP is the third door into the same real system. How I implemented WebMCP Imperative API: document.modelContext.registerTool , with a provideContext fallback for hosts that shipped the earlier surface. Plain JavaScript, no dependencies, no framework. Tool results use the MCP content shape. Verified end to end in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, and with the Model Context Tool Inspector extension driving the tools through a real agent loop. Safety, in this order: the page never books without a human click; no modelContext means no behavior at all; agent input is never parsed as markup, because the confirmation card is built with createElement only. Server-side validation, rate limits and junk filters are shared verbatim with every other door. Built and run by Serhii Kravchenko, https://github.com/awrshift Built With astro cloudflare javascript mcp node.js sqlite webmcp Try it out yesmcp.com github.com mcp.yesmcp.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo entry. I built the WebMCP layer on top of my own production booking service: the six tools and their schemas, the confirmation card that keeps the final click with the human, and the demo video. The backend has been running since August 21, and the WebMCP work was done during the submission period.
